caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Bolivia entered the period unusually strong: debt fell from 48.6% of GDP in 2006 to 30.5% in 2011 on HIPC-era relief and the gas boom. It then climbed almost every year as gas revenues faded and deficits became structural: 31.8% in 2014, 48.9% in 2019, 67.5% in 2020 on COVID, 78.3% in 2023, 83.2% in 2024, and a projected 84.8% in 2025. The headline ratio understates the strain, since the central bank financed deficits by drawing down reserves while the official peg masked the monetary expansion. GDP in dollar terms barely grew from $39.3bn in 2014 to a projected $64.3bn in 2025, so the debt burden is real, not a denominator illusion. The next administration faces the classic choice: fiscal consolidation and devaluation, or continued reserve depletion.
inflation_management: Bolivia was Latin America's low-inflation outlier for most of the period, an artifact of the fixed exchange rate (6.86 bolivianos per dollar since 2011) and heavy fuel subsidies rather than of monetary credibility. Inflation spiked to 14% in 2008 and 9.9% in 2011 on food and commodity prices, then stayed under 6% from 2012 through 2024, including 1.8% in 2019, 0.7% in 2021, and 2.6% in 2023. The model broke in 2024-25: dollar and fuel shortages, a parallel exchange rate far above the official peg, and subsidy cuts pushed inflation to 5.1% in 2024 and a projected 19.5% in 2025 - the highest in the series. With international reserves reportedly near exhaustion and the peg undefended in practice, the new government inherits an exchange-rate regime in name only.

key_events.event: Evo Morales took office; gas nationalization funded a decade of high spending.
Commodity super-cycle: gas and mineral revenues drove rapid GDP growth and debt reduction.
Oil and gas price collapse ended the boom; fiscal surpluses turned to persistent deficits.
Disputed October election led to Morales's resignation in November and an interim government.
COVID-19; Luis Arce (Morales's former economy minister) won the October election.
Attempted military coup in June amid dollar and fuel shortages; economic crisis deepened.
Rodrigo Paz won the October runoff with 54.5%, ending nearly 20 years of MAS rule; inflation projected at 19.5%.

outlook_next_decade: Bolivia is at a genuine inflection point: the gas-and-subsidy model is exhausted and the October 2025 election handed a center-right government a mandate for change. The base case is a painful but necessary adjustment - devaluation, subsidy reform, and IMF engagement - that restores stability within a few years and opens lithium and mineral investment. The risk is that adjustment without a social cushion replays the unrest of 2019, and that depleted reserves force a disorderly rather than orderly transition. Watch the exchange rate: a unified, credible FX regime is the single best predictor of whether the new era sticks.
